You are a rigorous speculative world-builder working for a film production. You
extrapolate societies forward two years at a time from a documented starting
state and a set of drivers that are stipulated as having come true. You are not
writing a thriller. You are writing the minutes of a world. Every change you
describe must have a visible mechanism; magnitudes must be defensible for a
two-year window; nothing happens because it is dramatic. Where the drivers pull
against each other, you show the friction rather than resolving it.

You write for an audience that includes an endocrinologist, a health economist,
a food-industry analyst and a political reporter. Any one of them should finish
your world and say "I don't like it, but I can't dismiss it."

It pays $199 a month now, only for people with severe obesity or a coded diagnosis, and it still drops anyone who misses five percent loss, eighty percent adherence or the annual bone scan. Six regional contractors are piloting connected pens that log each dose. Body inequality has moved from weight to body composition, where generics do not help.\"],\"still_true\":[\"The CMS continuation standard's terms are unchanged: ≥80% PDC, six-monthly verified weigh-ins, ≥5% loss at 6 months or clinician override, annual DEXA for long-term 65+ users, and the 90-day bone-pause code.\",\"Exactly 31 states plus DC have adopted the continuation standard for the 90% Medicaid match; no state joined or left.\",\"Retatrutide's list price remains $1,499 a month.\",\"The FTC consent orders still bar 'anxiety treatment' claims for low-dose subscriptions while 'calm' and 'focus' wording remains permitted.\",\"The suicidal-ideation warning removed from Wegovy, Zepbound and Saxenda labels in January 2026 has not returned.\"]}", "prose": {"headline": "Thin Is Generic Now: The $39 Pen, the Hidden Fracture Memo and America's New Hunger for Muscle", "world_in_600_words": "At the end of 2034 a little more than one American adult in four is on an incretin drug, and for many of them it is now a forty-dollar purchase. Generic semaglutide arrived in February 2033, on the date Novo had agreed with the generic makers two years earlier. By the end of that year seven companies were shipping it, most of them Indian. The weekly pen that cost $199 on the federal portal now costs $39 to $69 at the pharmacy counter. It is cheap enough that the money question has mostly gone away. What remains is whether someone has an hour, a clinician and a scanner.\n\nEmployers drew their own conclusion from the falling price. A drug that costs about as much as a gym membership looked to many benefits managers like something employees could pay for themselves, and the fracture data made the coverage look like a liability. During 2033 and 2034 the share of employers covering weight management fell from two-thirds to about four in ten. What is still covered is mostly filed under diabetes, heart, sleep-apnea or kidney codes. The people who were dropped mostly did not quit. About ten million of them moved to cash generics, many after a few months of regain, and now inject outside every monitoring system the government built. Medicare and the thirty-one Medicaid states still require verified weigh-ins and annual bone scans. A woman of fifty-six paying cash at Kroger has no such requirement and no one checking.\n\nThe bone problem has become a story about trust. In September 2033 Novo settled the Justice Department's civil case for $2.4 billion. Documents released with the settlement showed that a 2029 internal analysis had found a roughly 40% higher fracture rate in older women and had never been sent to the FDA. The company's US chief resigned. The agency strengthened fracture language across the class and ordered every sponsor to reanalyse its bone data. It also refused Amgen's monthly MariTide until the company produces two years of bone-density data. Claims analysts now estimate about fourteen and a half thousand excess hip fractures a year among long-term older users. Bone-scan waits have shortened as mobile vans multiply, but the vans serve the insured.\n\nThe needle no longer stands in anyone's way. In March Lilly's high-dose Foundayo tablet matched injectable semaglutide head to head, at $129 a month. That makes it the premium way to get a result the generic pen gives for less. Novo's answer to the generics was a new indication. In April the FDA approved oral semaglutide for gambling disorder. The same action wrote reduced reward responsiveness into every incretin label as an uncommon, dose-related side effect, so the flattening that 'calm' subscriptions sold as a feature now carries a warning. The big HR platform has since moved 'focus' products out of its standard catalogue. Subscribers have fallen from three and a half million to under two and a half.\n\nThe cheaper thinness gets, the less it signifies. Among people under forty in Austin, Brooklyn and Los Angeles, the body that now signals money and time is dense: muscle you can see, a good lean-mass score on the scan, and an appetite you show off at dinner.
